raw_text:
### Introduction and Mechanism of Action
Heart failure (HF) remains a major global public health challenge with high morbidity and mortality. For decades, therapeutic strategies focused exclusively on blocking neurohormonal pathways that promote pathological cardiovascular remodeling, such as the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) and the sympathetic nervous system. However, the introduction of angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibition (ARNI) marked a fundamental paradigm shift by simultaneously enhancing protective compensatory mechanisms. Sacubitril/valsartan, the first-in-class ARNI, consists of the neprilysin inhibitor prodrug sacubitril and the angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB) valsartan [1]. 

Neprilysin is a zinc metallopeptidase that degrades a variety of endogenous vasoactive peptides, including atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP), brain natriuretic peptide (BNP), and C-type natriuretic peptide [2]. By inhibiting neprilysin, sacubitril increases the concentration of these natriuretic peptides, facilitating vasodilation, natriuresis, diuresis, and the inhibition of hypertrophy and fibrosis. Simultaneously, the valsartan component selectively blocks the angiotensin II type 1 ($\text{AT}_1$) receptor, preventing the deleterious vasoconstricting and profibrotic effects of angiotensin II [3]. This dual-acting mechanism provides superior neurohormonal modulation compared to traditional RAAS blockade alone.

### Clinical Evidence in HFrEF
The clinical efficacy of sacubitril/valsartan in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) was established by the landmark PARADIGM-HF trial [4]. In this prospective, double-blind trial, 8,442 patients with HFrEF were randomized to receive either sacubitril/valsartan (200 mg twice daily) or the angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor enalapril (10 mg twice daily) on top of standard therapy. The trial was stopped early due to overwhelming clinical benefit, showing a 20% relative risk reduction in the primary composite endpoint of cardiovascular death or hospitalization for heart failure (hazard ratio [HR], 0.80; p < 0.001) [4]. Further analyses of PARADIGM-HF revealed that sacubitril/valsartan significantly delayed clinical progression [5], reduced the risk of sudden cardiac death [6], and improved health-related quality of life compared to enalapril [9]. 

The mechanism behind these clinical benefits was further elucidated by the PROVE-HF and EVALUATE-HF trials. PROVE-HF demonstrated a strong correlation between the reduction of N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) levels and significant cardiac reverse remodeling, as evidenced by improvements in left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) and volumes [7]. Concurrently, EVALUATE-HF showed that sacubitril/valsartan improved aortic impedance, indicating a reduction in arterial stiffness [8].

### In-Hospital Initiation and Advanced Heart Failure
Following the success in chronic HFrEF, the clinical utility of ARNI therapy was extended to acute decompensated heart failure (ADHF) through the PIONEER-HF trial [10]. Among patients hospitalized for ADHF, initiating sacubitril/valsartan in-hospital after hemodynamic stabilization led to a significantly greater reduction in NT-proBNP levels compared to enalapril, with comparable safety and tolerability. Long-term follow-up from PIONEER-HF confirmed a substantial reduction in the secondary endpoint of rehospitalization for heart failure [11]. 

The TRANSITION study supported these findings, demonstrating that initiating sacubitril/valsartan either in-hospital or shortly after discharge was highly feasible and safe [12], while the TITRATION trial provided a clinical framework for safe up-titration over 3 to 6 weeks [13]. For patients with advanced, end-stage HFrEF, however, the LIFE trial showed that sacubitril/valsartan did not offer a statistically significant improvement in NT-proBNP or clinical outcomes compared to valsartan, highlighting therapeutic limitations in end-stage refractory populations [14].

### Extending Therapy Across the Ejection Fraction Spectrum
To evaluate ARNI therapy in patients with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), the PARAGON-HF trial randomized 4,822 patients to receive either sacubitril/valsartan or valsartan alone [15]. While the trial narrowly missed statistical significance for its primary endpoint of total HF hospitalizations and cardiovascular death (HR, 0.93; p = 0.059), substantial heterogeneity in treatment response was observed. Post-hoc pooled analyses of the PARADIGM-HF and PARAGON-HF trials showed that the clinical benefits of sacubitril/valsartan extend up to an LVEF of approximately 55% to 60%, with particularly pronounced efficacy in women [16,17]. 

The PARALLAX trial further confirmed that sacubitril/valsartan significantly reduced NT-proBNP levels compared to individualized medical therapy in HFpEF [18], and subsequent analyses demonstrated a slower decline in renal function [19,20]. In contrast, in the acute post-myocardial infarction setting (PARADISE-MI), sacubitril/valsartan did not show a statistically significant reduction in cardiovascular death or incident heart failure compared to ramipril, although it was associated with a favorable safety profile [21].

### Cardiorenal Protective Effects and Safety Profile
Beyond cardiovascular benefits, sacubitril/valsartan has demonstrated significant cardiorenal protective properties. In PARADIGM-HF, patients treated with the ARNI had a slower rate of decline in the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and a lower incidence of renal failure compared to those on enalapril [22]. Similar renal protection was noted in diabetic patients, along with improved glycemic control and reduced insulin requirements [23]. Data from chronic kidney disease trials, such as UK-HARP III, also supported its renal safety profile [24]. 

In daily practice, hypotension remains the most common adverse event associated with sacubitril/valsartan, though this rarely leads to treatment discontinuation, even in patients with low baseline systolic blood pressure [25]. Importantly, concerns regarding possible cognitive impairment due to impaired amyloid-beta clearance in the brain were resolved by the PERSPECTIVE trial, which confirmed no adverse impact on cognitive function over a 3-year period [26].

### Guidelines, Real-World Data, and Implementation
Reflecting this robust clinical evidence, major international clinical guidelines have established sacubitril/valsartan as a foundational therapy (Class I recommendation) for patients with HFrEF [27,28]. Accumulating real-world evidence from registries such as Get With The Guidelines-Heart Failure (GWTG-HF) has confirmed the safety, tolerability, and clinical benefits of ARNI therapy in clinical practice outside the rigorous setting of clinical trials [29]. Furthermore, health economics evaluations have consistently demonstrated that sacubitril/valsartan is highly cost-effective, driven by a marked reduction in hospital readmission rates and a substantial increase in quality-adjusted life years [30].
